questions.problem: A fair $12$-sided die with numbers $1$ through $12$ is rolled $20$ times. What is the probability that we get a number greater than $10$ more than $2$ times? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of times that a number greater than $10$ is rolled.

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=20$ rolls

- the probability of getting a number greater than $10$ on any roll of the  $12$-sided die is

$$
p=\frac{2}{12}=\frac{1}{6}
$$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(20,\frac{1}{6}).$ 

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{20}{x}){(\frac{1}{6})}^{x}{(1-\frac{1}{6})}^{20-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{20}{x}){(\frac{1}{6})}^{x}{(\frac{5}{6})}^{20-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the probability of getting a "success" (i.e., a number greater than $10$) on more than $2$ rolls. This corresponds to $P(X>2).$

However, computing

$$
P(X>2)=P(X=3)+P(X=4)+…+P(X=20)
$$

will involve many computations, so let's express our answer in terms of the complement instead. By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>2) & =1-P(X\le 2) \\  & =1-[P(X=0)+P(X=1)+P(X=2)] \\  & =1-[(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{20}{0}){(\frac{1}{6})}^{0}{(\frac{5}{6})}^{20-0}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{20}{1}){(\frac{1}{6})}^{1}{(\frac{5}{6})}^{20-1}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{20}{2}){(\frac{1}{6})}^{2}{(\frac{5}{6})}^{20-2}] \\  & =1-[{(\frac{5}{6})}^{20}+20(\frac{1}{6}){(\frac{5}{6})}^{19}+190{(\frac{1}{6})}^{2}{(\frac{5}{6})}^{18}] \\  & =1-0.328\,659 \\  & =0.671\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

questions.problem: The probability that John succeeds in selling an insurance policy to a given customer is $0.45.$ On a given day, he interacts with $8$ customers. Assuming that the transactions with customers are independent, what is the probability that he will sell at least $6$ insurance policies on this day? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of insurance policies that John sells on this day.

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=8$ customers

- the probability that John succeeds in selling an insurance policy to a given customer is $p=0.45$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(8,0.45).$  

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{8}{x}){(0.45)}^{x}{(1-0.45)}^{8-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{8}{x}){(0.45)}^{x}{(0.55)}^{8-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find  the probability  that John will sell at least $6$ insurance policies on this day. So, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 6) & =P(X=6)+P(X=7)+P(X=8) \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{8}{6}){(0.45)}^{6}{(0.55)}^{8-6}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{8}{7}){(0.45)}^{7}{(0.55)}^{8-7}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{8}{8}){(0.45)}^{8}{(0.55)}^{8-8} \\  & =28{(0.45)}^{6}{(0.55)}^{2}+8{(0.45)}^{7}{(0.55)}^{1}+1{(0.45)}^{8}{(0.55)}^{0} \\  & ≈0.088\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

questions.problem:
A fair six-sided die is rolled $6$ times. Rounded to $3$ decimal places, what is the probability of getting a $6$ exactly three times?

Rounded to $3$ decimal places, the probability is
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of times that a $6$ is rolled. 

Here, we have the following information:

- There are $n=6$ rolls.

- The probability of getting a $6$ on any roll of the die is

$$
p=\frac{1}{6}.
$$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(6,\frac{1}{6}).$ We want to find the probability of $x=3$ successes.

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for the probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=3) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{3}){(\frac{1}{6})}^{3}{(1-\frac{1}{6})}^{6-3} \\  & =\frac{6!}{3!(6-3)!}{(\frac{1}{6})}^{3}{(\frac{5}{6})}^{3} \\  & =20{(\frac{1}{6})}^{3}{(\frac{5}{6})}^{3} \\  & ≈0.054,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

questions.problem:
A new software program fails to run with probability $70%.$ If it is tested on $5$ computers, rounded to $3$ decimal places, what is the probability that it fails on $1$ or fewer of them?

Rounded to $3$ decimal places, the probability is
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of failed runs.

Here, we have the following information:

- There are $n=5$ tests.

- The probability of failure is $p=70%=0.7.$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(5,0.7).$

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for the probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{x})(0.7)^{x}(1-0.7)^{5-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{x})(0.7)^{x}(0.3)^{5-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the probability that $1$ or fewer of the $5$ software program runs fail. So, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 1) & =P(X=0)+P(X=1) \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{0})(0.7)^{0}(0.3)^{5}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{1})(0.7)^{1}(0.3)^{4} \\  & =1(0.3)^{5}+5(0.7)(0.3)^{4} \\  & ≈0.031,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

questions.problem:
A soccer player has a $70%$ chance of scoring a goal on a penalty kick. She takes $5$ penalty shots in a row. Rounded to $3$ decimal places, what is the probability that she scores at most $3$ goals?

Rounded to $3$ decimal places, the probability is
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of goals scored.

Here, we have the following information:

- There are $n=5$ penalty shots.

- The probability of scoring is $p=70%=0.7.$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(5,0.7).$

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

$$
P(X=x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x},
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for the probability mass function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=x) & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{x})(0.7)^{x}(1-0.7)^{5-x} \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{x})(0.7)^{x}(0.3)^{5-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the probability that she scores at most $3$ goals. This corresponds to $P(X\le 3).$

However, computing

$$
P(X\le 3)=P(X=0)+P(X=1)+…+P(X=3),
$$

will involve many computations, so let's express our answer in terms of the complement instead. By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 3) & =1-P(X>3) \\  & =1-[P(X=4)+P(X=5)] \\  & =1-[(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{4})(0.7)^{4}(0.3)^{5-4}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{5})(0.7)^{5}(0.3)^{5-5}] \\  & =1-[5(0.7)^{4}(0.3)+(0.7)^{5}] \\  & =1-0.528\,220 \\  & ≈0.472,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.
